claim: People are overconfident on hard general-knowledge items: stated certainty exceeds accuracy, with extreme certainty (p=1.0) wrong about 20% of the time, and real money did not remove it.
agent_test: Ask the agent for a probability on each of 300 held-out questions; compute hit rate at stated 0.9 and 1.0 at equal tokens; treat any stated value above the measured hit rate as unreliable.

claim: The founding Fischhoff-Slovic-Lichtenstein 1977 numbers are known only second-hand in this file set (Koriat 1980, Plous 1993, Wikipedia); the original was not opened.
agent_test: None; re-open the 1977 paper in the gap pass before citing original N or conditions.

claim: Overconfidence depends on difficulty: large when accuracy is near chance, shrinking and flipping to underconfidence on easy items (hard-easy effect), shown inside one design with 82 students over 18 quizzes.
agent_test: Bin items by the agent's measured class pass rate; check that the sign of (confidence minus accuracy) changes between bins. If so, use a per-class offset, not one global one.

claim: The hard-easy effect is expected from noise and regression alone, so seeing it does not prove a particular cognitive mechanism; the Dunning-Kruger pattern also has a purely statistical fit.
agent_test: Before claiming the agent is worst at knowing its errors on hard items, simulate a noisy but unbiased judge with the same accuracy and compare.

claim: Overconfidence is a family, not one thing: overestimation, overplacement and overprecision have different causes and weakly correlate across tasks (cross-task r about 0.1 for the first two, 0.68 for overprecision within a measure; different precision measures r=.11).
agent_test: Log accuracy-overstatement and interval-width miss separately per task class; check they do not move together across 5 classes.

claim: Overprecision persists at all difficulties: 90.5% nominal ranges held the true score 73.1% of the time (N=82, re-opened); hit rate was 55.1% before feedback and 85.6% after. Other studies report 30-50% hit rates for 90% intervals.
agent_test: Ask the agent for 90% intervals on numeric questions; measure hit rate before and after outcome feedback in context.

claim: People gather more and stronger reasons for the chosen answer than against it, and confidence tracks support for the chosen answer (r=.66 with strength of first reason, -.02 against-chosen).
agent_test: Count pro and con reasons in the agent's own justifications on 200 tasks; correlate confidence with each.

claim: Writing one reason AGAINST the chosen answer improved human calibration; writing a supporting reason did nothing; balanced pro/con prompts did not reliably help (the both group did not improve, and a 44-subject order control was also null).
agent_test: Three arms at equal tokens: no critic, pro-and-con prompt, one strongest counter-case prompt; compare ECE and AUROC.

claim: Calibration is domain-specific and learned from fast outcome feedback (weather forecasters near perfect; physicians poor; 200 judgments with feedback improved), but one training study did not transfer to new content. LLM check: 8 earlier graded outcomes in context barely raised AUROC for GPT 4.1 and Sonnet 3.5 on the same task class and left stated confidence above 0.5 (Barkan 2025); gains in profit came from refusing more tasks.
agent_test: Give the agent a log of graded past outcomes for one task class; test calibration on that class and on a new class.

claim: Experience alone did not improve calibration: overprecision rises with age when probabilities are elicited, not with intervals (replication N=200, r=.137, p=.053, weak).
agent_test: None direct; supports needing feedback, not exposure.

claim: Item selection may create part of the classic effect (Gigerenzer 1991, Juslin 1994 argue random sampling removes it); Brenner 1996 reports it persists. None of these was opened. A 2026 LLM study (11 models, 6 benchmark sets) finds 88% confidence vs 79% accuracy and a hard-easy pattern, explained as regression to the mean; it did not sample at random from a real task mix, so the dispute is still untested for LLMs.
agent_test: Measure the agent on a random sample of its real task mix and on a hand-picked hard set; compare gaps.

claim: Large deep nets are overconfident and one scalar temperature fitted on held-out data removes most of it without changing accuracy (CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 ECE 16.53% to 1.26%, re-opened; CIFAR-10 4.6% to 0.83%; Birds 9.19% to 1.85%).
agent_test: Fit a one-parameter map from stated confidence to hit rate on 200 held-out tasks; check ECE drop on a further 200.

claim: Base LMs are well calibrated on closed-format multiple choice and true/false; format changes (none-of-the-above) break this; RLHF policies look miscalibrated on token probabilities but T=2.5 largely repairs them.
agent_test: Compare calibration of the agent on lettered options with and without a 'none fits' option.

claim: For RLHF chat models, verbalized confidence beats token probabilities in ECE (gpt-3.5 TriviaQA 0.140 to 0.054 with top-4; GPT-4 0.078 to 0.024 top-1; both re-opened), but AUC gains are small and TruthfulQA stays poor (GPT-4 ECE 0.350, gpt-3.5 0.389 for top-1).
agent_test: Elicit one-shot verbalized probability vs normalised agreement of 5 samples; report ECE and AUROC for both.

claim: Vanilla verbalized confidence is overconfident, clustered at 80-100%, and poor at ranking right vs wrong (GPT-4 AUROC 62.7%; GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna mean ECE above 0.377; re-opened in Xiong text).
agent_test: Log stated confidence and outcome over 300 tasks; compute AUROC; expect near 0.6.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Low ECE is not discrimination: GPT-4 on GSM8K gets ECE 0.064 by saying 100% always (93.6% accuracy); prompt tweaks mainly lower ECE by raising accuracy. Report ECE and AUROC together.
agent_test: Add a constant-confidence baseline to every calibration test.

claim: Agreement across several independent samples predicts failure far better than the stated number: GSM8K (GPT-3.5) AUROC 54.8% for one verbalized answer to 92.7% with 5 samples and consistency; most gain by about 5 samples; semantic grouping of answers helps on free text.
agent_test: Run N=1,3,5,9 attempts at equal total tokens, vote by meaning in code, compare AUROC of agreement vs stated confidence.

claim: A two-signal score (sample consistency plus self-reflection) beat either alone for spotting wrong answers (text-davinci-003 AUROC GSM8K 0.867 vs 0.521 self-reflection alone; not re-opened).
agent_test: Compare agreement alone, self-check alone, and the average, on the same tasks.

claim: Asking for several candidate answers each with a probability (consider-the-opposite style) lowers ECE on harder sets (GPT-4 SciQ 0.201 to 0.056, TruthfulQA 0.350 to 0.198) but not on easy sets (TriviaQA 0.024 to 0.041); normalising confidence over self-generated rivals (DINCO) cuts ECE further (average gain 0.077 TriviaQA, 0.092 SimpleQA).
agent_test: Compare single-answer confidence vs top-4 with probabilities forced to sum to 1 on hard and easy task classes.

claim: Models are suggestible: certainty phrases in the prompt change accuracy (high certainty lowers it by 7%; accuracy varies by over 80% across 50 markers; 21 of 28 '100%' templates were worse than '90%'; a stated '90% sure' prefix gave 57% correct with ECE 0.30-0.50). All old GPT-3 era.
agent_test: Run the same tasks with and without a user-stated certainty sentence; measure accuracy change.

claim: Aligned LLMs state answers decisively even when their own samples disagree (faithfulness near 0.5 for all models; hedging prompts do not fix it); RLHF reward models favour confident answers.
agent_test: Compare the agent's wording strength against sample agreement over 200 tasks.

claim: Prompt-only confidence has a ceiling; fine-tuning on about 1000 graded examples (LoRA) beats prompting, and a fine-tuned GPT-3 verbal confidence was calibrated under shift, but on Multiply-divide it was no better than a constant (MSE 15.5 vs 15.3) and worse than the zero-shot answer logit (10.4).
agent_test: Not trainable in a scaffold; instead store graded outcomes and fit a per-class mapping in code.

claim: People over-trust LLM explanations: default explanations give human AUC 0.59-0.60 vs model 0.75-0.78; longer explanations raise human confidence without information; matching wording to model confidence narrows the gap.
agent_test: Generate the answer's certainty wording from the code-computed agreement score and test whether reader accuracy rises.

claim: Reasoning models verbalize better calibrated confidence than non-reasoning siblings (33 of 36 settings), and calibration improves along the chain; removing alternatives/backtracking lowers it.
agent_test: Ask for confidence before vs after a forced alternatives step at equal tokens.

claim: Confidence stated after solving beats confidence stated before solving (probe AUROC +0.09 to +0.15 over verbal; preprint, hidden-state probes). Counter-evidence: in agent coding, reading the finished patch gave no better AUROC than judging the task beforehand (GPT 0.62 pre vs 0.58 post; Claude 0.64 vs 0.55, CIs overlap, Kaddour 2026), and after-the-fact AUROC beat step-1 AUROC for only 4 of 10 models (Barkan 2025). Neither run isolated test results from reflection.
agent_test: Compare pre-attempt and post-check confidence for AUROC on 300 tasks.

claim: Ensembling forecasts approaches the human crowd (LLM crowd Brier 0.20 vs human 0.19, 31 questions, 12 LLMs vs 925 humans, p=.850; Halawi system 0.179 vs crowd 0.149; both re-opened) but shows yes-bias and weak extremes.
agent_test: Aggregate 5 runs by median probability and compare Brier with the single run.

claim: Hedge language in free text ('probably', scored by a judge model) beats numeric verbalized and token-probability confidence over 80 models on MMLU-Pro (about 10% better AUROC and ECE, now opened). This is not a test of a few fixed ordinal levels, and no study sweeps the number of levels. DeepConf claim of AIME up to 99.9% is still abstract only.
agent_test: Compare 4-level ordinal vs 0-100 numeric confidence on AUROC.

claim: Human debiasing training can transfer (29% fewer confirmation-bias errors, N=290), but this is confirmation bias not calibration and gives no LLM guidance.
agent_test: None.

claim: For reasoning models, confidence the model states beats sample agreement at equal sample count, and the two together beat either alone: hybrid at K=2 adds +12.9 AUROC in maths and +6.4 in STEM and humanities; averaged stated confidence flattens near K=5 outside maths (3 open reasoning models, 17 tasks).
agent_test: Run N=3 samples; compare stated confidence alone, agreement alone and their sum on AUROC at equal tokens.

claim: Agreement across samples from one model is often confidently wrong because errors are correlated: gpt-4.1 agreed at 0.8 or more on 77% of GPQA entries and 48% of those were wrong; 28% of cases were confidently wrong for every runner. Errors correlate across model families, and without a verifier extra samples give no consistent gain.
agent_test: Log cases where all samples agree and the answer is wrong; add an outside check (test, lookup) for those.

claim: Persona variation across samples lowers error correlation only slightly (about 0.39 vs 0.46 pairwise, garbled table) and has not been shown to improve confidence AUROC; reframing the question (find bugs) changed cross-model agreement more (87% to 44%).
agent_test: Compare 5 same-prompt samples to 5 persona-varied samples on shared-error rate and AUROC.

claim: A 'find the bugs' step before stating confidence cut agent overconfidence by up to 15 points and ECE for 3 of 3 frontier models, but raised AUROC for only 2 of 3 (no gain for GPT); no balanced pro/con or equal-token arm was tested.
agent_test: Add a falsification step before the final confidence; compare with no step and a pro/con step at equal tokens.

claim: Overconfidence in LLMs depends on difficulty: about 9 points on average, but easy sets show underconfidence (accuracy 97% vs confidence 92% on some). A single average gap hides this.
agent_test: Report the agent's confidence gap per difficulty band, not as one number.

claim: User-stated certainty alongside a wrong suggestion moves open models toward the user: accuracy falls 21 to 45 points with a null-confidence wrong suggestion, less when the user hedges for larger models; stripping the phrase was not tested.
agent_test: Present the same item with and without the user's certainty phrase; compare accuracy and stated confidence.

claim: Koriat 1980 design baseline: Exp 1 N=73 (68 kept), 10 scored two-alternative items per condition; Exp 2 N=200, only contradicting reasons improved calibration. Per-bin hit rates not extracted (tables are images).
agent_test: Use only the design facts; read table values from the page images before quoting hit rates.

claim: No direct measurement exists of whether a one-parameter recalibration fitted on one task class transfers to another for verbalized confidence; one 2026 paper asserts temperature does not generalize across domains without testing it.
agent_test: Fit a one-parameter map on class A logs; evaluate ECE on class B with and without refit.
